html:
The Battle of Dunkirk was fought from 26 May to 4 June 1940 around the port of Dunkirk in northern France, early in World War II. The German army had trapped the British and French armies against the sea, but about 338,000 soldiers were carried to England by ship.

On 10 May 1940 Germany attacked in the west. Its tanks cut through the Ardennes forest and reached the English Channel in ten days, splitting the Allied armies. The British army in France fell back on Dunkirk. On 24 May the German tanks were ordered to halt for three days; historians still argue why. The Royal Navy sent every ship it could, joined by hundreds of fishing boats, ferries and pleasure craft. The Royal Air Force fought the German bombers overhead. French troops held the edge of the pocket to the end, and about 40,000 of them were captured.

The British saved their trained soldiers but left nearly all their guns and vehicles. France signed an armistice on 22 June. Churchill warned that wars are not won by evacuations, yet without those men Britain could hardly have fought on. Next came the Battle of Britain.
